Knight versus bishop: evidence on winning

1,769,562 records scanned across April–September 2026, 48 distributed random-byte windows and 48 observed dates. Both players rated at least 500.

Actual outcomes

55,663

Three different populations. Captures use the general hash sample, engine rates use evaluated moves, and actual outcomes use all qualifying equal-material bishop-versus-knight positions found in the windows. Sample sizes must not be added together. The source archives were sampled, not exhaustively scanned.

Overall findings

Actual outcomes do not establish an overall winner. The metrics describe different aspects of contribution.

Captured material per player-game: knights 3.55 / bishops 4.10 pawn-equivalent points from each pair of original pieces.

Geometric influence: knights 3.53 / bishops 3.72 attacked squares per original piece per position. Legal mobility: knights 2.44 / bishops 2.49 destinations per original piece on its owner's turn. Captured pieces contribute zero thereafter; overlapping attacks count per piece.

Engine winning chance lost per evaluated move: knights 4.02 / bishops 4.14 percentage points; lower is better.

Cumulative signed engine change per original piece per qualified player-game: knights -11.45 / bishops -10.38 percentage points, in 359,021 player-games with at least 80% adjacent-evaluation coverage. This sums changes after that piece's own moves; negative values record lost chances, and move frequency affects the total.

Adjusted bishop-minus-knight actual win probability: +0.08 percentage points, 95% interval [-0.75, +0.90]. Raw win rates: knights 46.20%, bishops 45.73%, draws 8.07%.

Actual outcomes are an adjusted observational association. Engine losses measure move execution. Neither assigns complete causal credit to a piece.

Lower bounds are inclusive and upper bounds exclusive: exactly 750 belongs to 750–1000. Captures are the pair's combined points per player-game. All loss/opportunity denominators, game counts and matched counts are retained. Sparse cells remain inconclusive; missing cells display —. Short games cannot qualify for the outcome checkpoints.

Record and normalize like the reference study

The preprocessing keeps immediate before/after evaluations, mover clock, owning-player rating, piece identity and valid opportunity counts. Rates divide event counts by all eligible piece moves in that bucket. The reduced SQLite databases and CSV normalizers allow new plots without downloading PGNs again.

What “winning contribution” measures here

Actual outcome comparison: each side has one original minor piece, bishop versus knight, and equal pawn/rook/queen counts. Both owners are in the same rating band and within 100 rating points. Select the first qualifying predeclared checkpoint after move 20 with at least two more full moves to follow.

Adjusted win probabilities use a regression of real wins against piece type, rating gap, colour, move number, material, pawn/king features, time-control pool and month. Holding those model features fixed provides a relative bishop-vs-knight contrast. Earlier trades, piece-square placement, unmeasured position details and player choices can still confound it.

Engine comparison: convert centipawns using the Lichess formula, compare immediately adjacent positions in the mover's perspective and record signed change and chance lost. A best move often maintains a chance already present. These move statistics do not capture all passive support or threats inducing an opponent's mistake.

Coverage, uncertainty and validation

The sampled source windows contain 1,769,562 records and span 48 observed dates. Total two-pass range transfers: 1.61 GB across archives totalling 175.7 GB. Random byte windows and complete-frame recovery are not an exact uniform sample of games. Raw archive payloads are kept only in RAM and released after processing.

Pointwise 95% capture and move-rate intervals use 1,000 archive-window bootstrap replicates. The actual-outcome model uses covariance clustered by window. No adjustment for multiple subgroup comparisons; repeated players across windows and selection into engine analysis remain limitations.

Outcome validation held out 11,264 games from 9 whole windows. Brier score 0.2457 versus constant baseline 0.2483; log loss 0.6844 versus 0.6897. The improvement over baseline is modest. Calibration and convergence are recorded.

Completed move count is not an outcome-model predictor. Splitting results by eventual length is descriptive and can introduce selection bias. Lichess ratings belong to separate time-control pools; pooled rows reflect the sampled mixture.
